source.title: Scaling Laws for Moral Machine Judgment in Large Language Models

record.file_problem: Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 are described, but their model-level data values are absent from the supplied text. The rest of the paper is readable and not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: Conceptual test of whether model performance scales predictably, using moral-preference distance rather than held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
record.gate_note: The paper reports scaling results for moral-judgment alignment. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, token-count or compute scaling, compute-optimal allocations, or controlled architectural differences. Per-model values are not present in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study reports how one downstream measure, distance from human Moral Machine preferences, changes with parameter count across 75 existing models. That is a new task setting for V6. It is cross-sectional across post-trained models from many families, not a controlled pretraining sweep. It measures no pretraining loss, tokens or compute, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors also claim that variance shrinks with scale, that the trend holds across families, and that the slow exponent (about 21% distance reduction per tenfold increase in size) means scale alone may not suffice without extended reasoning.
record.recipe_differences: Measures distance from human Moral Machine preference vectors across existing model configurations, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy or controlled pretraining sweeps over parameters, tokens, and compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment is also associated with reasoning capability, and the reasoning effect varies with model size. Model family is included as a random effect; the paper reports family-specific negative trends but notes differing statistical power and parameter-range coverage.
record.problems: Model size is not experimentally isolated from correlated factors, and proprietary parameter counts are estimates from published literature. The outcome is a distance-based alignment metric whose practical significance the authors say needs human evaluation. The reported model-level supplementary values are absent from the supplied text, limiting extraction to aggregate results.
record.rows_left_out: No separate row for each model configuration could be extracted because the supplied text describes Table S1 but does not include its model-level values. No held-out cross-entropy, token-count, compute-budget, or controlled architecture result is reported.

untested.parts: Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss; extrapolation of downstream performance to larger models; tasks other than Moral Machine dilemmas; controlled scaling within a single training recipe.
Not tested: no pretraining loss is measured.
Not tested: no fixed-size shape comparison.
Not tested: no other modalities or training regimes.
Not tested: no comparison of fitting choices or exponent dependence.

missing.what: Size coefficient across nested mixed models A–D (−0.096, −0.096, −0.101, −0.120), showing that the estimate depends on which covariates are included.
Family-specific size slopes: described as 'predominantly negative', with random-slope SD 0.017, 8–19 models per family; no per-family values are given.
Release date adds nothing beyond size (LRT χ²=0.10, p=0.76), and residuals are uncorrelated with release date (ρ=0.047, p=0.69).

record.verdict_notes: The evidence is cross-sectional across heterogeneous post-trained models. Proprietary parameter counts are literature estimates, cited to a medical benchmark paper (ref 16). Reasoning models were evaluated on 5,000 rather than 10,000 scenarios. Size is confounded with training recipe, so the study cannot isolate scale. It is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss is not measured.
No small-run fits are used to predict much larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation or compute-optimal trend is tested.
Architecture details are not varied under controlled fixed-parameter comparisons.
The study does not compare modalities or the listed training regimes.
Only Moral Machine life-death dilemma alignment is assessed; other downstream tasks and prediction from pretraining loss are not tested.
The paper compares functional forms, but does not test how exponents or allocations change under different fitting choices, nor report curves bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: 75 model configurations (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Instruction-tuned or chat-optimized variants were prioritized; standard and extended-reasoning models were included.
rows.operation_detail: Related model parameter count to Euclidean distance between model and aggregate human AMCE preference vectors.

conditions.value: Moral Machine; 10,000 scenarios for standard models and thinking-disabled models, first 5,000 for reasoning-focused and thinking-enabled models

rows.measure: Euclidean distance from human preferences versus model size; Spearman rank correlation and fitted power law
rows.uncertainty: Power-law exponent α = 0.10 ± 0.01; p = 1.8 × 10−13 for Spearman correlation
rows.note: Aggregate result across the 75 configurations. Lower distance indicates closer alignment with the human preference vector.

rows.subject: 75 model configurations (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Instruction-tuned or chat-optimized variants were prioritized; standard and extended-reasoning models were included.
rows.operation_detail: Compared the power-law fit of distance against model size with alternative functional forms.

conditions.value: Power-law compared with linear, logarithmic, and exponential forms

rows.measure: Goodness of fit for distance versus model size
rows.value: Power-law R2 = 0.50; linear R2 = 0.16; exponential R2 = 0.19; power law exceeds the next-best logarithmic fit by ΔR2 = 0.03
rows.note: The paper reports the power law as the best-fitting tested form, with a small fit advantage over the logarithmic form.
rows.check: The power law (R²=0.50) beats the logarithmic form (R²=0.47) by only ΔR²=0.03, so the data barely tell the two apart. The functional-form claim is weak, so 'observed' overstates it.

rows.subject: 75 model configurations (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Instruction-tuned or chat-optimized variants were prioritized; standard and extended-reasoning models were included.
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the model-size association with alignment in a mixed-effects model controlling for release date, reasoning capability, and family-level intercepts and slopes.

conditions.value: Release date, reasoning capability, model family, and size×reasoning interaction

rows.value: Model size β = −0.120, SE = 0.016, p < 0.001; the paper reports this as corresponding to a power-law exponent α = 0.12
rows.note: The coefficient is from the model controlling for family, release date, reasoning, and the size×reasoning interaction.
rows.check: The model-size coefficient varies across nested models (−0.096 to −0.120, Table S4). Model size has only about 5.9 df because there are just 5 families. The row cites only Model D.

rows.subject: 75 model configurations (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Instruction-tuned or chat-optimized variants were prioritized; standard and extended-reasoning models were included.
rows.operation_detail: Compared alignment by reasoning capability and estimated its interaction with model size.
rows.measure: Reasoning effect and size×reasoning interaction on moral-preference distance
rows.baseline: Standard models; direct distance values not stated
rows.value: Reasoning β = −0.156, SE = 0.044, p = 0.001; size×reasoning β = 0.057, SE = 0.025, p = 0.024. The reasoning advantage was more pronounced in smaller models.
rows.uncertainty: SE = 0.044 and p = 0.001 for reasoning; SE = 0.025 and p = 0.024 for the interaction
rows.note: This shows that reasoning capability also predicts alignment and that its association varies with size.
rows.check: The row mixes the reasoning main effect, which is not a size-scaling result, with the size×reasoning interaction. The interaction (+0.057 on a size slope of −0.120) roughly halves the size slope for reasoning models. Size scaling is therefore weaker in that subgroup.

rows.subject: 75 model configurations (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: Instruction-tuned or chat-optimized variants were prioritized; standard and extended-reasoning models were included.
rows.operation_detail: Inspected the spread of alignment distances across model sizes.
rows.measure: Variation in moral-preference distance around the fitted trend
rows.value: The paper states that variance decreases with model size and that larger models cluster more tightly around the power-law trend.
rows.note: The variance observation is based on visual inspection; no separate numerical dispersion estimate is reported.

relationships.condition: All 75 configurations, 0.27B–1000B, Moral Machine distance vs parameter count
relationships.reason: Distance falls with size (Spearman ρ=−0.73, exponent 0.10±0.01, r1). The trend survives family, release-date and reasoning controls (β=−0.120, r3), and spread narrows at larger sizes (r5).
relationships.display_finding: Judgment distance decreased with size with Spearman ρ=−0.73 and exponent 0.10±0.01, retained a size effect of β=−0.120 after controls, and became less variable at larger sizes.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: All 75 configurations, 0.27B–1000B, Moral Machine distance vs parameter count
source_check.reason: r1 shows decreasing distance with size; r3 retains a negative size coefficient with controls; r5 records the authors' qualitative observation of decreasing spread.

relationships.condition: Precision and functional form of the size trend
relationships.reason: Size explains only half the variance (R²=0.50). The power law and the logarithmic form fit almost equally (0.50 vs 0.47), so the relation is noisy and its form is not identified (r1, r2).
relationships.display_finding: Size explained half the variance, with nearly equal fits for power-law and logarithmic forms at R²=0.50 and 0.47.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Precision and functional form of the size trend
source_check.reason: r1–r2 qualify predictive precision: the power-law regression has R²=0.50 on log-transformed distance. Its small reported fit advantage over the logarithmic form limits confidence in the particular function; V6 itself does not require a power law.

relationships.reason: The positive size×reasoning interaction (β=0.057) roughly halves the size slope for reasoning models. Reasoning mode shifts distance independently of size (β=−0.156) (r4).
relationships.display_finding: A size–reasoning interaction of β=0.057 roughly halved the size slope, while reasoning mode independently shifted judgment distance by β=−0.156.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: r4 shows reasoning-dependent scaling: the positive interaction offsets approximately half the negative standard-model size slope. The reasoning main effect is conditional on size, rather than a constant improvement across sizes.

relation.reason: Its own correlation, fitted scaling relationship and mixed-effects results directly test V6.

tranche.reason: Reports a size–performance relationship in a new downstream setting: alignment with aggregate human Moral Machine preferences across existing model configurations.

source_check.notes: Cross-sectional associations do not isolate causal effects of scale; proprietary parameter counts are estimates. Reduced spread is a visual observation, and practical moral-judgment benefits beyond correspondence with aggregate human preferences remain unvalidated.

statements.correction: Moral Machine: 75 configurations; Spearman ρ=−0.73, p=1.8×10−13; fitted D∝S^(−0.10±0.01), R²=0.50; family, release-date and reasoning controls; coefficient standard errors reported; GitHub repository linked. Royal Society Open Science review status: unverified in supplied text. Out-of-sample forecasting validation: not reported.
statements.problem: The direction and correlation are correct, but the supplied text does not establish peer review or publication in Royal Society Open Science. Any blanket claim that forecasting functions are absent also needs qualification: this study reports a fitted power-law function.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: All 75 tested model configurations on the Moral Machine evaluation
reader_labels.reason: Alignment distance decreases with size with a fitted power law and a strong negative rank correlation (r1); among the tested functional forms, the power law fits best (r2), and the adjusted size effect remains negative (r3).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Comparisons across standard and extended-reasoning model configurations
reader_labels.reason: Reasoning capability is independently associated with better alignment, with a larger advantage at smaller sizes, so alignment is not explained by size alone in this setting (r4). The study tests only one downstream evaluation framework.
